text: This is the formula at the centre of every transformer, as it was written in the paper that introduced the architecture. You already know most of it: queries meet keys, softmax turns scores into weights, and the weights mix the values. Two pieces are new, a division by the square root of the key width and a mask added to the scores, and to understand why they are there we first need to look closely at softmax itself.

Softmax exponentiates every score and divides by the total. The exponential makes every weight positive and keeps the order, so a larger score always gets a larger weight. More subtly, the ratio between two weights depends only on the difference between their scores, because e to the a divided by e to the b is e to the a minus b. Adding the same number to every score therefore changes nothing, and that is a gift, because a computer that tries to exponentiate a score of a thousand will overflow. So we subtract the largest score first, like measuring everyone's height from the tallest person rather than from sea level: the differences, which are all that matter, stay the same.

The spread of the scores controls how decisive softmax is. Multiply all the scores by a large number and the biggest one takes almost all of the weight, so softmax behaves like picking the maximum. Shrink the scores towards zero and the weights become nearly equal. That is where the name comes from: softmax is a soft, adjustable version of choosing the largest entry.

Now the scaling. Suppose the entries of a query and a key are random numbers of ordinary size. Their dot product adds up one product per dimension, so its spread grows with the width: with sixty four dimensions, the typical score is about eight times larger than with one. Scores that large push softmax into its decisive regime before training has learned anything, the weights become almost one hot, and a saturated softmax passes back very little gradient. Dividing every score by the square root of the key width brings the spread back to about one, whatever the width, so learning can start gently.

Next, the mask. A language model is trained to predict every next token in a passage at once: position one predicts position two, position two predicts position three, and so on, all in one parallel pass. That only works if no position can see the answer, so each token may attend to itself and to earlier tokens, but never to later ones. It is like reading with a card that covers the rest of the page.

The mask is applied before softmax by adding minus infinity to every score above the diagonal. The exponential of minus infinity is exactly zero, so those positions receive no weight at all, while each row still sums to one over the positions that remain. The weight table becomes lower triangular: the first token can only look at itself, and the last token can look at everything before it.

Put together, scaled dot product attention runs in five steps on a table that keeps the same square shape throughout. Multiply queries by keys, divide by the square root of the key width, add the mask, apply softmax to each row, and multiply by the values. Each step is a plain array operation, and you will write all of them in a few lines of NumPy.

One head of attention can only learn one way of looking, though. A word may need to find its subject, the word before it, and the end of the last sentence, all at the same time. The next lesson runs several heads side by side, each with its own queries, keys and values, and that is multi head attention.
